title: Unemployment & Safety Nets
description: The help that exists when income stops, and how to use it.
wolfLine: Even the strongest wolf leans on the pack sometimes.

unemployment-insurance.definition: State-run payments that replace part of your wages for a while if you lose your job through no fault of your own.
unemployment-insurance.example: About half your old weekly pay, up to a state maximum, for up to 26 weeks in many states.

snap.definition: A government program, often called food stamps, that gives people with low income monthly money for groceries on a card.
snap.example: $250 a month loaded onto a card for groceries.

medicaid.definition: Free or low-cost health coverage for people with low income. Rules differ by state.
medicaid.example: Coverage after a job loss drops your income.

hardship-program.definition: Lower or paused payments a company offers when you’ve lost income. You usually have to ask.
hardship-program.example: Your phone company pausing half your bill for two months after a layoff.

lessons.title: Unemployment Insurance
lessons.summary: What it is, who gets it, and how long it lasts.

steps.context: [[Unemployment insurance]] pays part of your old wages for a while if you lose your job through no fault of your own. Each state runs its own program.
steps.prompt: Who usually qualifies?
choices: People laid off through no fault of their own
Anyone who quits for any reason
steps.explain: It’s for losing work you didn’t choose to lose.

steps.prompt: Unemployment is run by your state, so rules and amounts differ from state to state.
steps.explain: Check your state’s labor department website.

steps.prompt: In many states, benefits last up to about…
steps.explain: About six months in many states. Some offer less.

steps.prompt: Unemployment benefits count as taxable income.
steps.explain: You can ask to have tax withheld, so April isn’t a surprise.

steps.prompt: To keep getting benefits, you usually must…
choices: Certify every week or two and look for work
steps.explain: Benefits come with a job search.

steps.prompt: Fired for serious misconduct. Unemployment?
steps.explain: It’s built for losing work through no fault of your own.

lessons.title: How Much You’d Get
lessons.summary: Usually helpful, rarely enough on its own.

steps.context: Many states pay roughly half your old weekly wage, up to a state maximum. These numbers are an example; check your own state.
steps.prompt: Your old pay was $900 a week. Half of that?
Your state’s maximum is $400 a week. What would you actually get?
steps.explain: The cap wins: $400.

steps.prompt: Over 26 weeks at $400?
Your essentials cost about $510 a week. What’s the weekly shortfall at $400?
So unemployment alone…
choices: helps, but usually isn’t enough by itself
steps.explain: Plan to combine it with savings and cuts.

steps.prompt: An emergency fund plus unemployment carries you much further than either alone.
steps.explain: Together they buy you months.

lessons.title: Applying for Benefits
lessons.summary: File early, report honestly, keep certifying.

steps.prompt: Put applying in order.
items: Apply on your state’s unemployment website right after losing your job
Answer questions about why you left
Report any work or pay you get
steps.explain: File, explain, certify, report.

steps.prompt: What do you usually need to apply?
choices: ID, Social Security number, and your recent employers and dates
steps.explain: Gather it before you start.

steps.prompt: If your claim is denied, you can usually appeal.
steps.explain: Read the letter for the deadline.

steps.prompt: You pick up a one-day job while on unemployment. What do you do?
steps.explain: Unreported pay can mean paying benefits back, plus penalties.

steps.prompt: Many states have a “waiting week.” What does that mean?
choices: The first week often isn’t paid
steps.explain: Another reason to apply right away.

steps.prompt: Applying late can cost you weeks of benefits.
steps.explain: Benefits usually start from when you apply, not when you lost the job.

lessons.title: Help With Food
lessons.summary: SNAP, food banks, and the number 2-1-1.

steps.context: [[SNAP]], often called food stamps, gives people with low income monthly money for groceries on a card.
steps.prompt: What can SNAP pay for?
steps.explain: Food from grocery stores.

steps.prompt: Losing your job can make you eligible for SNAP, even if you never were before.
steps.explain: Eligibility is based on current income.

steps.prompt: Where else can you get food help fast?
steps.explain: Often same-day help.

steps.prompt: Dialing 2-1-1 in most of the US connects you to…
choices: Local help with food, housing and bills
steps.explain: A free line to local programs.

steps.prompt: Using SNAP or a food bank during a hard stretch is exactly what they’re for.
steps.explain: No shame in using a safety net.

steps.prompt: SNAP covers $280 of your $400 grocery budget. How much does that free up for other bills?
steps.explain: The $280 you’d have spent on food can go elsewhere.

lessons.title: Health Coverage When Money Is Tight

steps.context: [[Medicaid]] is free or low-cost health coverage for people with low income. Rules differ by state.
steps.prompt: When might you qualify for Medicaid?
choices: When your income drops, like after a job loss
steps.explain: It’s based on current income.

steps.prompt: Kids may qualify for low-cost coverage through CHIP, even if their parents don’t.
steps.explain: CHIP covers kids in families that earn too much for Medicaid.

steps.prompt: Where do you check Medicaid and Marketplace options?
steps.explain: Start at the official sites.

steps.prompt: Marketplace plans can come with discounts based on your income.
steps.explain: Lower income, bigger discount.

steps.prompt: Your income drops to zero mid-year. Smart move?
choices: Check Medicaid and the Marketplace right away
steps.explain: Losing income can open the door.

steps.prompt: Which usually costs least for someone with very low income?
steps.explain: Often free.

lessons.title: Talking to Landlords and Lenders
lessons.summary: Call before you miss a payment, not after.

steps.context: Many companies have [[hardship programs|hardship-program]]: lower or paused payments when you’ve lost income. You usually have to ask.
steps.prompt: When should you call?
steps.explain: You have more options before you fall behind.

steps.prompt: Rent is due in 10 days and you were just laid off. Best move?
choices: Talk to your landlord now and propose a payment plan in writing
steps.explain: Landlords prefer a plan to a surprise.

steps.prompt: Utility companies often have payment plans or assistance programs.
steps.explain: Ask before the shut-off notice.

steps.prompt: When money is short, which bills come first?
choices: Housing, utilities, food and getting to work
steps.explain: Keep a roof, the lights and food.

steps.prompt: Pay first, or can it wait?
items: Car insurance, if you need the car

steps.prompt: A payment plan agreed in writing protects you better than a promise on the phone.
steps.explain: Get it in an email at least.

steps.title: Survival mode, on purpose
steps.body: A bare-bones budget covers only what keeps you housed, fed, healthy and able to find work. Everything else pauses until income is back.

steps.prompt: Keep or pause in a bare-bones month?
Plan a bare-bones month on $2,000 from unemployment and savings. Rent is fixed at $1,100.
steps.explain: Essentials first, and every dollar has a job.

steps.prompt: Your normal month costs $3,100. Bare-bones costs $2,000. How much less is that?
With $8,800 of savings covering bare-bones spending, how many full months does it last?
Cutting to bare-bones early stretches savings the furthest.
steps.explain: Every early dollar saved buys time later.

lessons.title: Ana’s Lean Months
lessons.summary: Benefits plus savings plus a plan.

story.title: Three lean months
story.body:
Ana’s call center closed in March. She applied for unemployment the same week and gets **$380** a week. She also qualified for **$250** a month in SNAP.

Her bare-bones costs come to **$2,300** a month, and she has **$3,000** saved.

steps.prompt: Unemployment for 4 weeks?
Add SNAP. How much help comes in a month?
What’s the monthly shortfall against her $2,300 of costs?
How many full months can her $3,000 cover that shortfall? Round down.
steps.explain: $3,000 ÷ $530 = 5.7, so 5 full months.

steps.prompt: What else could stretch Ana’s money?
choices: Asking her phone company and utilities about hardship programs
steps.explain: Every bill lowered adds time.

steps.prompt: Ana’s plan works partly because she applied for help early.
steps.explain: Applying the same week meant no lost weeks of benefits.

lessons.title: Sharpen Up
lessons.summary: Smart repetition on what you’re closest to forgetting.

lessons.title: Den Trial: Safety Nets
lessons.summary: 8 questions. Three strikes and you’re out.

steps.prompt: Your old pay was $800 a week. Your state pays half, up to $375. What’s your weekly benefit?
steps.explain: Half would be $400, but the $375 cap wins.

steps.prompt: Unemployment benefits are taxable income.
steps.explain: Have tax withheld, or set some aside.

steps.prompt: What does SNAP pay for?
steps.explain: Food.

steps.prompt: When should you call a lender about a hardship program?
steps.explain: Early calls open more doors.
